feed.title: Articles: why homes get messy, and where to start | 6S Success
feed.subtitle: Long form articles on why cleaning does not last, where to start when the house feels like too much, what 6S is, and how long a room really takes.

entry.title: What is 6S? The six steps, and how it differs from 5S
entry.summary: 6S is Sort, Straighten, Shine, Safety, Standardize, Sustain, in that order. What each step does, why Safety is fourth, and how it differs from 5S.

entry.title: How long does it actually take to organise a room? | 6S Success
entry.summary: Real session times for all 20 rooms, summed from the 114 micro zones. A room is 3 to 7 sessions, not one afternoon, and that is why whole-room attempts fail.

entry.title: Why you always lose your keys, and the fix that works
entry.summary: Losing your keys is not a memory problem. It is a missing assigned home. One tray, placed where your hand actually opens, in one session.

entry.title: Why does the medicine cabinet never get cleared out?
entry.summary: A medicine cabinet never smells off the way food does, so nobody notices it needs checking. The trigger that works, and the item most likely to hurt a guest.

entry.title: Why does mail always pile up by the door?
entry.summary: A mail pile is not a filing problem, it is undecided paper. Give every piece a verdict, act, file, or recycle, with a deadline, and it stops forming.

entry.title: Why do you have to move three things to get the one you need?
entry.summary: The thing you want is not missing, it is buried behind or under three others. Too many steps is its own root cause, distinct from no home or poor reach.

entry.title: Why can't you ever find the right charger?
entry.summary: A drawer of tangled chargers is not clutter, it is a missing home per device. One strip, one named slot each, and what to actually do with the old phone.

entry.title: Is that really a backup, or are you just storing it?
entry.summary: A backup only counts if it has actually covered for the main one. The one question that tells a real backup apart from something you are just storing.

entry.title: How to organize a junk drawer (and keep it that way)
entry.summary: A junk drawer is not a failure, it is an unnamed drawer. Give it a category, a written list, and a dated overflow box, and it stops refilling itself.

entry.title: Why you start organizing and never finish
entry.summary: Picking a small zone was the right move. Why the session still stalls anyway, and the four changes that fix finishing rather than starting.

entry.title: Why tidy is not the same as safe
entry.summary: A tidy zone can still hurt someone. Why unsafe placement is its own root cause, separate from clutter, and the three step check that catches it.

entry.title: Why is the thing you use every day the hardest one to reach?
entry.summary: The everyday pan lives under two others. Poor accessibility is a distinct root cause, and the fix is simple: match height to how often something is used.

entry.title: Why doesn't anything fit here, even after you declutter?
entry.summary: Sometimes a zone is not disorganized. It is genuinely too small for what it honestly needs to hold. How to tell the difference, and what to do once you know.

entry.title: Why does the same spot never actually get clean?
entry.summary: The blinds, the fridge top, the range hood filter. Not skipped from laziness. Skipped because reaching them costs more than everything else combined.

entry.title: Why does it live in one room but get used in another?
entry.summary: An item can have a real, assigned home and still cause clutter, because the home sits in the wrong room. Wrong location is its own root cause, with its own fix.

entry.title: Why does everyone disagree about what counts as clean?
entry.summary: Clean is not a fact, it is a guess, so two honest people can look at the same counter and reach two different answers. Fix it with a standard that is specific.

entry.title: Why does a shared zone never stay reset?
entry.summary: A zone several people use can fail even when everyone is willing, because nobody specifically owns resetting it. Here is the fix, and how to assign it.

entry.title: Why do you keep running out of things without noticing?
entry.summary: You are not careless. A full cabinet hides a low count as well as it hides an empty one. Give the zone a line, not a count, and the surprise stops.

entry.title: Why can't you see the clutter in your own house anymore?
entry.summary: Guests notice the pile by your door the second they walk in. Why your own eyes stopped flagging it months ago, and the three checks that make it visible again.

entry.title: How long should you keep something you can't decide about?
entry.summary: A fair, workable answer to the maybe pile: tag it, give it a decide-by date matched to what it is, and let time make the call instead of forcing a guess.

entry.title: Why your family won't put things back where they belong
entry.summary: It is rarely willingness. Why a system only one person maintains fails, and how to make putting things back the easier choice for everyone in the house.

entry.title: Why you keep buying things you already own
entry.summary: Duplicate cans, three half-used bottles, a fourth pack of batteries. Overbuying is a visibility problem, not a willpower problem, fixable at home.

entry.title: Why everything needs an assigned home
entry.summary: A surface with room on it is not a home. Why no assigned home is the most common root cause behind clutter, and how to give everything in a zone exactly one.

entry.title: How to declutter sentimental items without the guilt
entry.summary: The guilt is not about the object. Why sentimental items stall Sort more than anything else, and five ways to decide, once, on purpose.

entry.title: Why your house gets messy again a week after you clean it
entry.summary: Cleaning is an event, and events expire. Why a clean room drifts back within a week, and the two things that hold it: a written standard and a reset trigger.

entry.title: Where to start decluttering when it all feels like too much
entry.summary: Start with one micro zone you can finish in a single session. How to pick your first using friction and effort, and why finishing small beats starting big.

entry.title: More storage will not fix a messy room
entry.summary: A bin cannot decide what stays, where it lives, or who owns it. Buying storage before diagnosing the problem just stores the mess a little longer.

entry.title: Decluttering vs. organizing: what's actually different
entry.summary: Decluttering decides what stays. Organizing decides where it lives. Mixing up the order is why a weekend of buying bins ends with the same stuff, tidier.

entry.title: What is a micro zone? The unit that actually gets organized
entry.summary: A room is too big to fix in one sitting; one object is too small to matter. A micro zone is the size in between: specific enough to diagnose and keep.
